A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SDP by the same authors. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and readable figures, support matching retained, revised and newly added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated-teacher experiments, cross-task transfer results, ablations and noisy-feedback tests in Section 5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulated-teacher experiments, a 16-participant human study, demographic analyses and an analysis of 45 preference-learning papers.

M1.justification: The two-phase SDP algorithm is retained. However, v1 Section 4.2 explicitly keeps reward-model hyperparameters fixed across phases, whereas v2 Table 1 specifies Tanh during reward pre-training and task-dependent Tanh or Leaky ReLU afterward. This is a limited reported model-configuration change; replacing zero with rmin otherwise expresses the existing minimum-reward convention.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cartpole-swingup to simulated evaluation and evaluates human feedback in Cartpole-swingup and Pendulum-swingup, introducing a new participant population. Door-open disappears from the main multi-algorithm benchmark but remains in transfer and state-distribution analyses, so it is not wholly removed.

E2.justification: v2 adds MRN and SDP + MRN throughout the preference-learning benchmark, extending the three existing preference algorithms to four. Appendix D.5 also evaluates a replay-buffer-only adaptation of Yu et al. (2022) against SDP. Existing scalar comparators and the SAC oracle remain.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes stated evaluation from five to ten episodes. Hyperparameter tables revise settings including Door-lock feedback frequency from 5,000 to 10,000 steps and Window-open SURF training counts from 50 to 200. The new human protocol introduces 40/48-query budgets and 300,000 training steps. These reported changes do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds participant-background analyses and the replay-buffer-only control. It removes v1's noisy-teacher tests, Cheetah-run feedback-budget sweep and several Door-open ablations. Most phase, zero-weight, fake-input, relabeling and transition-quality analyses are retained and relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five simulation seeds, 95% confidence intervals and Welch tests at the 0.05 threshold. v2 adds numerical p-value columns to preference-result tables and reports statistical comparisons between participant groups. No increase in simulation seed counts is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds MRN, Cartpole, human-study and survey results while revising many existing preference scores. For example, Cheetah-run SDP + PEBBLE final return changes from 735.31 in v1 Table 5 to 704.63 in v2 Table 11 under revised reported evaluation settings, not a demonstrated same-setting decline. Scalar means are retained. Some v2 significance findings remain uncertain because Figure 2 and Table 14 disagree for Door-unlock and Window-open.

T1.justification: v2 introduces Equation 4, formally defining the intended sub-optimal trajectories through rewards within epsilon of the minimum at every step. v1 describes low-quality data informally. The existing reward-learning mathematics remains substantially unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution—using pseudo-labeled low-quality data to improve feedback efficiency—remains unchanged. v2 extends the stated validation claims to real human teachers and explicitly claims real-world applicability in the introduction and conclusion. This refines the claimed applicability without replacing the central methodological contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantial discussion of simulated-versus-human feedback, demographic generalization and usability by non-experts. It acknowledges insufficient participants for racial-group comparisons and clarifies that unavailable true rewards prevent directly checking the new sub-optimality criterion. The transfer discussion now emphasizes similarity to target-task pre-training rather than primarily outperforming PEBBLE.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link and a promised anonymized human-data release. Appendices provide participant instructions, practice procedures, interface details, survey-selection criteria, and human-study and MRN hyperparameters. Additional SAC settings and phase-specific reward-model configurations expand the technical documentation beyond v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds a structured survey of 45 preference-learning papers and positions human evaluation and participant diversity as important research gaps. It incorporates additional work on bi-level optimization, active querying and synthetic-teacher reliability, and empirically distinguishes SDP from the previously cited offline approach of Yu et al. (2022).

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: preference experiments precede scalar experiments, research questions are consolidated and explicitly linked to results, implementation discussion moves into experimental design, and several main-text ablations move into organized appendix subsections. The introduction, related work and conclusion are revised around human evaluation, with appendices reorganized into A–D.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. v1's composite Figure 4 is distributed across several figures, preference charts incorporate MRN and Cartpole, and new human-study violin plots and interface images appear. Dense result tables are split by metric and suite, with additional survey and demographic tables.

improvement.justification: The human study on two simulated tasks addresses an important weakness of v1: evaluating a human-feedback method only with scripted teachers. Together with the MRN comparison, direct offline-method control and detailed human-study documentation, it substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility. The gains are qualified by small demographic groups, removal of noisy-teacher tests, and conflicting significance labels between Figure 2 and Table 14. These issues limit particular claims but do not outweigh the substantial benefit of direct human-feedback evidence.
